Series::grouped_var¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::grouped_var(
    const Series& group_ids,
    std::int64_t group_count,
    std::int64_t ddof = 1) const -> Series

What It Does¶

grouped_var() returns the variance of the values within each group.

For a group with members x of size k and mean m, the result is

sum_i (x_i - m)^2 / (k - ddof)

computed in the numerically stable “sum of squares minus square of sum” form and then clamped at 0 so that rounding cannot produce a small negative variance.

  • self is a 1-D Series of values, length n

  • group_ids is a 1-D label per value, same length, each label in [0, group_count)

  • entry g of the length-group_count result is the variance over the values labelled g

The default ddof = 1 is the sample (unbiased) variance, dividing by k - 1. Pass ddof = 0 for the population variance, dividing by k. This default is the opposite of the moving-window movvar, which always uses population normalization.

Parameters¶

group_ids (const Series&)

A 1-D label per value, any integral or boolean dtype, each in [0, group_count). Out-of-range or negative labels raise.

group_count (std::int64_t)

The number of output groups, >= 0.

ddof (std::int64_t, default 1)

The delta degrees of freedom. The divisor is group_size - ddof. Must be >= 0.

Returns¶

Series A 1-D Series of length group_count, dtype float64 on CPU (float32 off-CPU). A group whose size is <= ddof (for example a one-element group with the default ddof = 1) divides by zero or a negative number and yields NaN. An empty group is also NaN.

Gradient¶

grouped_var() is differentiable. The sensitivity of a group’s variance flows back to each member proportionally to its deviation from the group mean.

Examples¶

Example 1. Two groups of four. Default ddof = 1.

auto values = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0});
auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.grouped_var(group_ids, 2));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 3.6667]

Group 0 is {2, 4, 4, 4} with mean 3.5, sum of squared deviations 3, divided by 4 - 1. Group 1 is {5, 5, 7, 9} with mean 6.5, sum of squared deviations 11, divided by 3.

Example 2. The same data with ddof = 0 divides by the group size instead.

auto values = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0});
auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.grouped_var(group_ids, 2, 0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.7500, 2.7500]

Example 3. A one-element group divides by 1 - 1 = 0 under the default and yields NaN.

auto values = pluss::make_series({5.0, 8.0, 2.0});
auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.grouped_var(group_ids, 3));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, nan, nan]

Example 4. An empty group is also NaN.

auto values = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 9.0});
auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 0, 1, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.grouped_var(group_ids, 3));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5000, 18.0000, nan]

Example 5. The backward pass. Each member’s gradient is proportional to its deviation from the group mean.

auto values = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0});
values.tracks_slope_(true);
auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

values.grouped_var(group_ids, 2).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[8], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000, 0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333, -1.0000, -1.0000, 0.3333, 1.6667]

Within each group the sensitivities sum to 0, because shifting every member by the same amount does not change the variance.

Example 6. An out-of-range label is rejected.

try {
  auto values = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
  auto group_ids = pluss::make_series({0, 9, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
  values.grouped_var(group_ids, 2);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::grouped_var: group id out of range; expected every id in [0, 2)

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The default is ddof = 1 (sample variance). Pass ddof = 0 for population variance. This differs from movvar, which is always population.

  • A group of size <= ddof, and any empty group, yields NaN.

  • The result is clamped at 0, so you will never see a small negative value from rounding, but you also cannot distinguish “exactly zero spread” from “clamped”.

  • The result is float64 even for an integer value column.

Summary¶

grouped_var() is the within-group variance:

  • entry g is sum (x - mean)^2 / (group_size - ddof) over values labelled g

  • ddof defaults to 1 (sample); pass 0 for population

  • one-element groups (default ddof) and empty groups are NaN

  • clamped at 0; differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::grouped_std: the square root of this.

  • Series::grouped_mean: the center this spread is measured around.

  • Series::var: the whole-series variance with no grouping.
